name: Lip-Teeth Synchronization
description: Analyzes lip and teeth coordination during speech — AI often fails to correctly render dental occlusion patterns.
mechanism:
This method detects deepfakes by analyzing the coordination between lip movements and teeth visibility patterns during speech, a subtle detail that AI generators consistently struggle with:

1. **Teeth Region Segmentation**: The method segments the mouth interior region using semantic segmentation, identifying: upper teeth, lower teeth, tongue, and dark mouth interior (oropharynx). For each frame, the method computes: (a) upper teeth visibility area — the pixel area of visible upper teeth normalized by mouth opening area, (b) lower teeth visibility area — similarly normalized lower teeth area, (c) teeth-to-mouth ratio — proportion of the mouth opening occupied by teeth vs. dark interior. Real teeth have fixed anatomical properties — they are rigid bodies that do not change shape, color, or size (though their visible area changes with lip position). The segmentation validates that teeth maintain consistent appearance identity across frames.

2. **Phoneme-Specific Dental Patterns**: Different speech sounds require specific lip-teeth configurations: (a) labiodental fricatives (/f/, /v/) require upper teeth touching lower lip (high upper teeth visibility, lower lip retracted), (b) dental fricatives (/θ/, /ð/ — 'th' sounds) require tongue visible between upper and lower teeth, (c) bilabial stops (/p/, /b/, /m/) require complete teeth occlusion (both teeth hidden behind closed lips), (d) open vowels (/a/, /æ/) show both upper and lower teeth with separation. The method correlates teeth visibility patterns with detected phonemes from the audio track and validates that the observed dental configuration matches the expected configuration for each phoneme class. Deepfakes frequently show incorrect dental patterns — teeth visible during bilabial closures, or no teeth during labiodental fricatives.

3. **Dental Occlusion Physics**: When the mouth closes (for bilabial consonants or swallowing), the upper and lower teeth must occlude — they come together in a specific bite pattern determined by the individual's dental alignment. The method tracks the occlusion process: upper and lower teeth should approach each other simultaneously and symmetrically, meeting at the occlusal plane. Real occlusion shows: upper teeth slightly overlapping lower teeth (normal overjet of 2–4 mm), consistent occlusion pattern across all closure events, and proper timing (teeth meet before lips close). Deepfakes often produce impossible dental occlusion — teeth that pass through each other, lower teeth overlapping upper teeth unnaturally, or teeth that disappear before the mouth fully closes.

4. **Teeth Identity Persistence**: Each person has a unique dental arrangement — tooth size, spacing, alignment, color variations, and any dental work (fillings, crowns) form a stable biometric signature. The method extracts a dental appearance feature vector from frames with maximum teeth visibility and tracks its consistency across the video. In authentic video, the dental feature vector has cosine similarity > 0.90 across all frames. Deepfakes — particularly face swap methods — may produce teeth that change appearance between frames: different tooth counts, changing gaps, shifting alignment, or color variations, because the generator synthesizes teeth independently per frame rather than maintaining a persistent dental model.
parameters:
Teeth segmentation: semantic segmentation (face parsing network)
Dental regions: upper teeth, lower teeth, tongue, oropharynx
Phoneme detection: audio forced alignment (Montreal Forced Aligner)
Labiodental phonemes: /f/, /v/ — upper teeth + lower lip contact
Bilabial phonemes: /p/, /b/, /m/ — full teeth occlusion required
Dental occlusion: overjet 2–4 mm, overbite 2–3 mm expected
Teeth identity: appearance feature vector, cosine similarity > 0.90
Minimum mouth resolution: 48×32 pixels
Frame rate requirement: ≥ 25 fps
accuracy: 80–89% accuracy detecting deepfakes via lip-teeth synchronization. Phoneme-dental correlation achieves AUC of 0.86 for face reenactment detection. Dental occlusion validation provides F1-score of 0.83. Teeth identity persistence achieves AUC of 0.88 for face swap detection. Performance is strongest for speech containing labiodental and bilabial phonemes and weakest for mumbled or closed-mouth speech.
source: Agarwal, S. et al. (2020). Detecting Deep-Fake Videos from Phoneme-Viseme Mismatches. Proceedings of CVPR Workshop on Media Forensics, 660–669.
useCase: Detecting face swap deepfakes through dental appearance inconsistency. Identifying lip-sync deepfakes through phoneme-dental mismatch. Forensic analysis of talking-head video testimony. Dental biometric authentication supplementing face recognition.
strengths:
• Teeth are rigid structures that provide stable biometric reference
• Phoneme-dental correlation provides content-dependent validation
• Dental identity persistence detects face swap inconsistency
• Occlusion physics provides absolute geometric constraints
• Works independently of face quality — targets specific anatomical detail
limitations:
• Requires visible teeth — closed-mouth subjects provide no signal
• Low-resolution mouth regions limit teeth segmentation accuracy
• Dental prosthetics, braces, or missing teeth may confuse the analysis
• Audio-visual alignment errors can cause false phoneme-dental mismatches
• Some languages have fewer labiodental phonemes, reducing analysis opportunities
